question: At a piston test cylinder, the rate at which the piston's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 4t^2 + 7t, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the total acceleration gained between t = 1 second and t = 2 seconds, and they multiply that acceleration by 4. That result acts on a connecting rod with a mass of 114,000 grams. (The cylinder head is cooled by 6 liters of coolant, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the push this rod requires, in newtons, then subtract 26 from that number, then subtract 23 more. Convert what remains into kilonewtons. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a satellite-thruster test bay crew reports, in kilojoules, comes from converting an energy value that had been reduced by 19. The unreduced energy, in joules, is what an 11 kilogram test mass carries while moving at a speed obtained by multiplying an earlier reading by 5. That earlier reading, in meters per second, is the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 14 and multiply together to give 48. (The thruster nozzle is 0.25 meters wide, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?

At a skateboard ramp test lab, a technician repeats a push-off test 3 times. Each run combines a baseline push worth 9 units with an extra kick worth 17 units, and adding the results from all 3 runs together gives the total speed, in meters per second, of a rider model with a mass of 21,000 grams. (The ramp's guard rail is painted with 4 liters of sealant, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the energy this model carries at that speed, in joules, then subtract 25 from that number, then multiply what remains by 4, and then add 21 more. What is the final number, in joules?

The final number a piston test cylinder crew logs, in newtons, is 26 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 24 less than a value that was, before that, multiplied by 3. Before that multiplication, the value was 28 less than a force reading a 37,000 gram connecting rod exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the total acceleration gained between t = 1 second and t = 4 seconds, given that the rate at which the rod's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = t^2 over that interval. (The cylinder bore measures 8 centimeters across, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in newtons?

A calibration sheet at a flywheel test rig lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a spinning test mass: the two numbers add up to 12 and multiply together to give 35. Records confirm the true reading is the larger of the two. That speed applies to a test mass with a mass of 30,000 grams. (The flywheel housing is bolted with fasteners rated at 60 newton-meters, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Add 19 to the result, then subtract 22, and then add 12 more. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a conveyor-belt test bench crew reports, in kilonewtons, is 25 more than a kilonewton figure obtained by multiplying a converted force reading by 9. That force, first in newtons, is what a 169 kilogram gearbox housing exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the smaller of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 8 and multiply together to give 15 -- after that force was multiplied by 2. (The conveyor belt itself is driven by a 4 kilowatt motor, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

The final number a robotics-lab technician records, in kilonewtons, is 7 more than an earlier figure, which is itself 3 more than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 70,000 gram test arm exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the number of different groups of 3 servo motors she could choose from 8 identical units on the shelf. (The shelf itself is 2 meters long, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a model-rocket sled test track, a sled's position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 - t^2, where t is the time in seconds after launch. Engineers need how sharply the sled's motion is changing at t = 1 second. That value applies as the speed, in meters per second, of a sled with a mass of 47,000 grams. Find the energy this sled carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 5. Convert what results into kilojoules, subtract 1 from the figure, and then multiply the result by 10. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

A calibration sheet at a flywheel test rig lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a spinning test mass: the two numbers add up to 5 and multiply together to give 4. Records confirm the true reading is the larger of the two. That speed applies to a test mass with a mass of 58 kilograms. Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then add 14 to that number, then multiply what remains by 12. Convert the result into kilojoules. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a satellite-thruster test bay crew reports, in newtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 9, and then by 9 again, after that figure had already been multiplied by 3 and by 5. The unmultiplied force is what a 65,000 gram thruster housing exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the smaller of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 6 and multiply together to give 5. (The thruster nozzle is rated for 12 volts, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in newtons?

The final number a piston test cylinder crew logs, in kilonewtons, is 28 more than an earlier figure obtained by multiplying a converted force reading by 12. That force, first in newtons, is 11 less than a reading a 172 kilogram connecting rod exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to its speed at t = 2 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 5t^3 - 6t^2 for t in seconds after ignition. (The cylinder bore measures 11 centimeters across, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At an elevator motor test rig, two support cables measure 190 centimeters and 124 centimeters. Technicians want the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both cables with nothing left over, and multiplying that length by 6 gives the speed, in meters per second, of a counterweight with a mass of 4,000 grams. (The elevator car is rated for 6 passengers, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this counterweight carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Add 28 to the result, and then subtract 11. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a wind-tunnel model test lab logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a kilojoule reading by 4, after that reading was reduced by 23. The unreduced kilojoule reading came from converting an energy value, in joules, carried by a 25 kilogram scale model moving at a speed gained between t = 0 and t = 2 seconds, given that the model's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 2t^2 + 2t over that interval. (The tunnel's intake fan is 1.5 meters across, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a flywheel test rig crew reports, in kilojoules, is 7 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 23 less than a value that was, before that, 12 more than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules. That joule value is the energy a 26 kilogram flywheel segment carries while moving at a speed equal to the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 5 and multiply together to give 6. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a water pump station crew reports, in kilojoules, is 6 more than a kilojoule figure obtained by multiplying a converted energy reading by 3. That energy, in joules, is what a 29,000 gram test slug carries while moving at a speed equal to the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 26 centimeter pipe segment and a 262 centimeter pipe segment with nothing left over. (The pump housing draws 750 watts, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?

A calibration sheet at a centrifuge rotor bay lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a spinning arm: the two numbers add up to 7 and multiply together to give 12. Records confirm the true reading is the smaller of the two. That speed applies to an arm segment with a mass of 59,000 grams. Find the energy this segment carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Subtract 20 from the result, then multiply what remains by 3, and then add 23 more. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a robotics-lab technician reports, in kilonewtons, is 1 more than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 25 kilogram test arm exerts while accelerating at a rate that is 2 more than the number of different groups of 4 servo motors she could choose from 6 identical units on the shelf. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a model-rocket sled test track, a sled's position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 - 3t^2, where t is the time in seconds after launch. Engineers need how sharply the sled's motion is changing at t = 3 seconds. That value applies as the speed, in meters per second, of a sled with a mass of 3,000 grams. Find the energy this sled carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 11, then subtract 7. Convert what remains into kilojoules. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a gear test bench crew reports, in newtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier force reading by 6. That force is what a 72 kilogram test gear exerts while accelerating at a rate obtained by multiplying an earlier reading by 3, and then by 5. That earlier reading, in millimeters, is the greatest length that divides evenly into both a 259 millimeter shaft and a 75 millimeter shaft with nothing left over. (The gearbox housing is cooled by a fan drawing 20 watts, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in newtons?

A calibration sheet at a flywheel test rig lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a spinning test mass: the two numbers add up to 5 and multiply together to give 6. Records confirm the true reading is the smaller of the two. Multiplying that speed by 11 gives the actual speed of a test mass with a mass of 20 kilograms. Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then add 28 to that number. Convert what results into kilojoules. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

The final number a pinball launcher test rig crew reports, in newtons, is 8 less than an earlier figure, which is itself obtained by multiplying a force reading by 3, after that reading was reduced by 4 and multiplied by 9. The unmultiplied force is what a 60 kilogram plunger head exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the total acceleration gained between t = 1 second and t = 3 seconds, given that the rate at which the plunger's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 4t^2 + 4t over that interval. What is the final number, in newtons?

At a satellite-thruster test bay, a technician repeats a burn test 5 times. Each burn combines a baseline thrust worth 9 units with an extra thrust worth 2 units, and adding together the results from all 5 burns gives the total speed, in meters per second, of a test mass with a mass of 3,000 grams. Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Add 8 to the result, and then multiply what remains by 11. What is the final number, in kilojoules?

At a conveyor-belt test bench, a technician repeats a load test 2 times. Each repetition combines a baseline load worth 2 units with an extra load worth 12 units, and adding together the results from both repetitions gives the total acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a gearbox housing with a mass of 18,000 grams. Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Multiply the result by 2, then subtract 20, and then multiply what remains by 10. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a gear test bench, two steel shafts measure 13 millimeters and 66 millimeters across their keyways. A technician wants the greatest length, in millimeters, that divides evenly into both measurements with nothing left over, and that length becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a test gear with a mass of 48,000 grams. Find the push this gear requires, in newtons, then add 7 to that number, then add 29 more, then multiply what remains by 12, and then convert the result into kilonewtons. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?

At a robotic-arm joint test bench, a joint's position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 - t^2, where t is the time in seconds after actuation. Engineers need the joint's speed at t = 1 second, and they add 23 to that speed to get the acceleration of a housing with a mass of 130,000 grams. (The housing's mounting plate is 0.9 meters across, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then subtract 6 from that number. Convert what remains into kilonewtons, and then multiply the result by 11. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
